title: Who Shares What From Whom: An Ego-Network Conjoint of Misinformation Sharing
summary: Who shares misinformation, and from whom? We ran a registered conjoint experiment with a YouGov sample of US respondents (12,000 profile ratings collected; models use 11,882 for sharing and 11,884 for plausibility). Each respondent saw a true or neutral headline, a false headline, or a fact-check, attributed to one of their real contacts, and chose whether to share it and rated its plausibility. Information type was randomized. Misinformation was chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral headlines (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]), and fact-checks 13.3 points less often (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]). A1. Source credibility is conditional on content uncertainty: the slope of sharing on trust in the sharer (1-5), net of the other source attributes, and how it differs by information type.
A1. The slope of plausibility on trust in the sharer, by information type.
A1. The close-tie premium on sharing, net of the other source attributes, by information type.

A2. Sharing without believing: among profiles chosen to share, the probability that the respondent judged the other post more plausible, by information type, net of source attributes, media trust and age. — Misinformation

A2. Sharing without believing: among profiles chosen to share, the probability that the respondent judged the other post more plausible, by information type, net of source attributes, media trust and age. — Fact-check

A3. Co-ideological messenger: sharing when the respondent and the sharer lean the same way (both liberal or both conservative) against opposite leans; pairs involving a moderate form a third group. Cell differences, no controls. — Congruent

A3. Co-ideological messenger: sharing when the respondent and the sharer lean the same way (both liberal or both conservative) against opposite leans; pairs involving a moderate form a third group. Cell differences, no controls. — Neutral (a moderate)

A4. Ego-network composition: the respondent's six named contacts as a measured network. Among misinformation profiles, sharing on the network's mean perceived belief in disputed claims, net of network ideological spread, mean trust, age and ideology. Each misinformation profile is weighted by 1 / the respondent's number of them, which reproduces the respondent-level regression of the misinformation-sharing rate.

B1. Message x respondent congruence: among partisan respondents shown partisan-slanted headlines, sharing of congenial against uncongenial content (headline slant from the paper's preliminary automated coding), by information type.
B2. A conspiracy-prone source: the slope of sharing on the sharer's perceived belief in disputed claims (0-1), net of the other source attributes, by information type.
B2. The slope of plausibility on the sharer's perceived belief in disputed claims, by information type.
B2, claim-specific (thin): for the anti-vaccine (polio) misinformation headline, plausibility when the sharer is seen as believing 'Covid-19 vaccines modify your DNA' against not.
B3. Health vs. political misinformation: among misinformation profiles, the trust slope on sharing for health (guanabana, polio) and political headlines.
B3. Among misinformation profiles, the close-tie premium for health and political headlines.
B4. Sharer origin (continental US vs. elsewhere) and sharing, by survey language and by the respondent's nativity.

extensions.label: Design advance
extensions.why: Fixes the design cause: randomizing attributes in vignettes turns the descriptive close-tie and high-trust contrasts into causal estimates and removes bundling with the real contact.
extensions.title: Randomize the sharer's attributes, with a behavioural share
extensions.hypothesis: H1: a randomized close tie raises the probability of sharing by about 0.03. H2: randomized high trust raises it by about 0.05. Both effects hold for false headlines.
extensions.primary_outcome: Share of the forwarded post to the mock feed (binary).

extensions.label: Generalizability
extensions.why: Fixes the missing_moderator cause: it pre-selects the moderator from S3 and S8 and tests it with enough power instead of relying on a tertile contrast.
extensions.title: Does the misinformation penalty hold across belief in disputed claims?
extensions.hypothesis: The gap in sharing between misinformation and true/neutral headlines is smaller among respondents in the top tertile of belief in disputed claims than in the bottom tertile (a positive infotype-by-moderator interaction). The penalty is present in both languages.
extensions.primary_outcome: Share: chosen/likely to share the headline (infotype x belief tertile interaction).

extensions.label: Theoretical debate
extensions.why: The retrieved literature (COVID, AI, media education) does not bear directly on sharing from ties, so I decline to invent a debate. Instead this brief tests the measurement cause: whether sharing and plausibility are distinct.
extensions.title: No debate visible in the retrieved works
extensions.hypothesis: The accuracy-salience prompt will narrow the misinformation sharing gap (false vs true/neutral) by at least 0.031 standard units relative to the control arm, while leaving the plausibility gap unchanged, demonstrating that sharing and plausibility are separable processes.
extensions.primary_outcome: Primary outcome: sharing intention, measured as a binary share/don't-share choice for each headline profile (same as source study). Secondary outcome: plausibility, measured on a 0–100 slider ('How plausible is this claim?') for the same profiles. The key estimand is the interaction between accuracy prompt and information type (false vs true/neutral) on sharing, tested against the null that the prompt does not differentially reduce sharing of false headlines. A secondary estimand is the same interaction on plausibility, expected to be null if the constructs are separable.

potential.verdict: A follow-up is worth running, but the headline-type effect is already settled and adds nothing new. The retrieved literature shows no genuine debate this study bears on, so the debate brief is replaced by a measurement test. Run the advance_design brief first: randomizing tie and trust with a behavioural share is the only way to turn the study's most interesting claims (close ties and high trust) into causal estimates. The moderator brief should follow, sized to the 0.056 subgroup gap.
